decisions.question: When a session has a predetermined narrative event, should the dice decide whether it happens?
decisions.commitment: No. A fixed event stays fixed and is written as a global event; what gets rolled is what the characters know about it when it lands. Understanding is the win condition, not occurrence.
decisions.why: Rolling whether the premise is true is a coin-flip on the premise, not a game — a 50% chance of 'the aliens do not come' makes the session incoherent rather than uncertain. The bombardment was already modelled this way and nobody objected to it: it happened to everyone, and the dice decided who survived it. The compound session extends the same shape to the arrival. Measured at N=400, the characters reach CERTAIN or CONVINCED about what is coming in 40.3% of runs and are BLIND in 7.5%, so the tension is real and lives entirely in the knowledge track.

decisions.question: Should a hazard's severity scale with how exposed a character is?
decisions.commitment: No. Severity belongs to the physical event and is the same for everyone standing in it; exposure controls how many separate incidents a character is in. A collapsing wall does not hit a trained person more gently.
decisions.why: The first NPC model put severity in the exposure tier and measured badly in both directions: four NPCs recorded zero deaths in 500 runs because their hit-point pool exceeded any single hazard's maximum roll and they could not be reduced to 0 at all, while a 4 HP commoner was killed by the SRD massive-damage rule before a death save was ever rolled. The SRD block choice was deciding every outcome and the exposure field was inert. Moving severity to the event and frequency to exposure (high = 3 incidents with a long rest between) made both ends behave: everyone can now die, and exposure is what drives the difference.
